executive_thesis:
In his *Expositio libri Posteriorum Analyticorum* (c. 1270–1272), Thomas Aquinas articulates his mature architecture of demonstrative science (*scientia*), taking geometry and arithmetic not merely as illustrative examples but as the primary realizations of the *most certain mode of demonstration* (*certissimus modus demonstrationis*, Lib. I, lect. 1). Because mathematical entities abstract from sensible matter and motion while retaining intelligible extension or discrete multitude, their demonstrations proceed solely from formal principles in which what is better known *in relation to us* (*quoad nos*) coincides with what is prior and better known *according to nature* (*secundum naturam*, Lib. I, lect. 4). Within this resolutory (*analytica*) framework, Aquinas resolves Plato's *Meno* paradox by distinguishing actual scientific knowledge (*scire simpliciter*) from the virtual pre-existence of conclusions within foreknown principles (*praecognitio*, Lib. I, lect. 2–3). Every demonstrative science requires three coordinated elements: a *subject-genus* (*genus subiectum*, such as continuous magnitude or number, of which both *what it is* and *that it is* are supposed), *proper attributes* (*passiones*, of which only nominal definitions are initially assumed while their inherence is demonstrated), and *common axioms* or *dignities* (*dignitates*, *communes animi conceptiones*, applied proportionally to the subject-genus, Lib. I, lect. 18). Crucially, Aquinas identifies Euclid's constructive problems—such as constructing an equilateral triangle upon a given finite straight line—as *quasi-operative demonstrations* (*demonstrationes quasi operativae*, Lib. I, lect. 2): in the order of construction the figure's mathematical existence is first demonstrated as a *proper attribute* of prior spatial elements, after which the constructed figure serves as a secondary *subject* for subsequent theorems, while singular diagrams such as a figure inscribed in a semicircle immediately yield actual science once recognized under their universal species (Lib. I, lect. 2–3).

Equally foundational is Aquinas's demarcation of the epistemological status of principles in Lectures 5 and 17–19. Whereas *axioms* or *common conceptions of the mind*—such as *If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal*—are self-evident both in themselves and to every intellect by inward reason alone, *positions* encompass unprovable nominal or quidditative definitions alongside propositional *hypotheses* (*suppositiones*) and *postulates* (*petitiones*), which are demonstrable in a higher science (ultimately first philosophy or natural philosophy) yet assumed without middle terms within geometry according to the learner's epistemic disposition (Lib. I, lect. 5, 17, 19). Against sophistical kind-crossing (*metabasis*), Aquinas exposes Bryson's attempted squaring of the circle as pseudo-demonstrative because its middle term exceeds the proximate genus of circle and rectilinear polygon (Lib. I, lect. 17). Against ancient skeptics and modern empiricists alike, he defends the exactitude of geometry in his celebrated analysis of *lines drawn in the dust* (*lineae in pulvere descriptae*, Lib. I, lect. 19): when the geometer calls a traced mark straight or one foot long, he utters no falsehood because he demonstrates neither *concerning* nor *from* sensible particulars, using visible figures solely as exemplars through which the intellect grasps universal natures existing *one in many* without needing Platonic separated Forms.

Finally, in the closing lectures of Book I and Book II, Aquinas unifies the downward apodictic hierarchy of mathematical exactitude with the upward inductive-abstractive genesis of first principles. Within the mathematical disciplines—ranked internally in Book I (lect. 41–42) by ontological simplicity from arithmetic's *unit without position* (*unitas sine positione*) to geometry's *point having position* (*punctus habens positionem*)—necessity holds *a priori* and universally, excluding both fortuitous events (*a fortuna*) and mere sensory observation (*per sensum*, Lib. I, lect. 42). Even if an observer stood upon the moon witnessing the earth's shadow or perceived by sight that a singular triangle's angles equal two right angles, he would still lack *scientia* until demonstration revealed the universal *per se* cause. Yet in Book II, Lecture 20, Aquinas shows that these universal principles are neither innate Platonic reminiscences nor arbitrary formalist conventions: from repeated sensations retained in memory, human collative reason forms *experience* (*experimentum*), from which the agent intellect abstracts the *universal resting in the soul* and awakens *understanding* (*intellectus*)—the infallible *habit of principles* that anchors all demonstrative science.

conceptual_table.significance: Designates the epistemic primacy of the mathematical sciences among human disciplines: because mathematics abstracts from sensible matter and argues strictly through formal principles, its premises are simultaneously better known to us and prior in nature.

conceptual_table.english_term: Foreknowledge (that it is / what it is)
conceptual_table.significance: Establishes the asymmetric prerequisites of demonstration: principles require foreknowledge *that* they are true, proper attributes require foreknowledge solely of *what* their names signify, and primary subjects (such as the unit or magnitude) require foreknowledge of both *what* they are and *that* they exist.

Aquinas's technical characterization of Euclidean constructive propositions (such as *Elements* I.1 and I.46), which demonstrate the mathematical existence (*quia est*) of composite figures like the equilateral triangle and square from presupposed lines and circles before proving further attributes of them.

conceptual_table.english_term: Axioms / Common conceptions of the mind
conceptual_table.significance: First indemonstrable propositions whose terms (such as *being*, *whole*, *part*, and *equal*) are grasped by all minds; they are evident to inward reason without external syllogism and are employed in geometry and arithmetic proportionally to their respective subject-genera.

Propositional principles asserting *to be* or *not to be* that are assumed without proof within a particular science (though provable by a higher science such as metaphysics or natural philosophy) and are readily assented to as probable by the learner.

Assumed propositional or constructive principles—exemplified by Euclid's postulate to draw a straight line from any point to any point—which the demonstrator asks the learner to grant when the learner holds neither prior assent nor contrary opinion.

The unified ontological domain of a science—discrete number for arithmetic, continuous magnitude for geometry—whose essential principles ground *propter quid* demonstrations and forbid illicit kind-crossing (*metabasis*) from alien genera.

Properties that flow *per se* and necessarily from the essence of the subject-genus (such as evenness and oddness in numbers, or commensurability, curvature, and angle-sum equality in magnitudes), defined with essential reference to their subject.

Refutes the empiricist and skeptical charge that geometry rests on false premises because drawn diagrams are neither perfectly straight nor exactly a foot long: sensible figures serve solely as phantasmatic exemplars, not as the logical premises or subjects of geometric proof.

conceptual_table.latin_term: Unitas sine positione / Punctus habens positionem
conceptual_table.english_term: Unit without position / Point having position
conceptual_table.significance: Captures the Aristotelian criterion of relative scientific priority by addition (*ex additione*): whereas the arithmetical unit is indivisible quantity without spatial site, the geometrical point adds determinate position in the continuum, ordering the *a priori* necessity of the mathematical disciplines.

conceptual_table.locus: Lib. I, lect. 42 & Lib. II, lect. 20
conceptual_table.significance: The collative synthesis of multiple singular memories by human particular reason, forming the indispensable cognitive bridge between transient sensation and the agent intellect's abstraction of the universal resting in the soul.

The supreme, unerring intellectual habit—distinct from discursive *scientia*—whereby the human mind, illuminated by the agent intellect upon the data of sense and experience, immediately apprehends first indemonstrable principles.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 1 — On the Necessity of Logic and the Most Certain Mode of Demonstration in the Mathematical Sciences
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Aquinas opens his commentary with a celebrated prooemium grounding the art of logic in the reflexivity of human reason. Because intellect and reason reflect upon their own operations, humanity requires an *art of arts*—logic—to direct the act of reasoning with order, ease, and freedom from error. Mapping the parts of the Aristotelian *Organon* onto the three operations of the intellect—simple apprehension of indivisibles (*Categories*), judgmental composition and division (*Peri Hermeneias*), and discursive reasoning—Aquinas divides discursive logic by analogy with nature's threefold causal efficacy (necessary, for the most part, and defective). The *judicative* or *analytic* (*resolutory*) part yields scientific certitude by resolving conclusions back to first principles: *Prior Analytics* secures formal syllogistic validity, whereas *Posterior Analytics* secures material necessity through *per se* propositions, standing above inventive logic (dialectic, rhetoric, poetics) and sophistic.

Turning to Aristotle's opening thesis—*Every intellectual teaching and learning comes about from pre-existing knowledge*—Aquinas contrasts Aristotelian causal realism with Platonic innate Ideenlehre. Just as natural agents genuinely educe forms from material potency rather than merely preparing matter to participate in separated Ideas, so demonstrative reasoning genuinely generates scientific knowledge from pre-existing cognition rather than merely removing impediments to recollection. Inductively verifying this principle across demonstrative sciences, dialectic, and rhetoric, Aquinas singles out the mathematical sciences as holding the principal rank among demonstrative disciplines because they possess the *most certain mode of demonstration* (*certissimus modus demonstrationis*).
key_theses: Logic is the reflexive *art of arts* directing the three acts of reason: simple apprehension, judgmental composition or division, and discursive inference.

The *Posterior Analytics* constitutes the material peak of *judicative* (*resolutory*) logic, achieving infallible scientific certitude by resolving conclusions into *per se* and necessary first principles.
Against Platonic reminiscence, intellectual teaching and learning genuinely generate new scientific knowledge in act from pre-existing cognition.
Among all demonstrative sciences, the mathematical disciplines hold first place on account of their *most certain mode of demonstration*.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 2 — On the Twofold Foreknowledge (That It Is and What It Is) of Subject and Attribute: Unit and Triangle
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Expositing Aristotle's doctrine of *foreknowledge* (*praecognitio*), Aquinas analyzes both *what* must be known prior to a scientific conclusion and the *order* in which it is known. Because every demonstrative conclusion predicates a *proper attribute* (*passio*) of a *subject* through a *principle*, foreknowledge distributes asymmetrically across the two fundamental questions *that it is* (*quia est*) and *what it is* (*quid est*). Principles, being complex enunciations (such as the principle of excluded middle), have no quidditative definition and require foreknowledge solely *that* they are true. Proper attributes cannot have their inherence (*quia est*) foreknown—for proving their inherence is the very task of demonstration—so one foreknows of them only *what is signified by the name* (*quid est quod dicitur*). Primary subjects, such as the *unit* in arithmetic or lines and surfaces in geometry, require foreknowledge of both *what* they are and *that* they exist.

To explain why Aristotle illustrates nominal foreknowledge of a proper attribute using the *triangle*, Aquinas introduces a pivotal distinction between sciences of substance and sciences of accidents like mathematics. In geometry, primary elements of quantity (unit, line, surface) are presupposed exclusively as subjects; from them, composite figures such as the equilateral triangle and the square are first demonstrated to exist through *quasi-operative demonstrations* (quoting Euclid I.1), where the triangle stands as a *proper attribute*, before subsequently serving as a *subject* for further theorems. Finally, Aquinas distinguishes principles foreknown *prior in time* (the universal major premise that every triangle has three angles equal to two right angles) from truths known *simultaneously in time* yet prior in nature—as when recognizing *this figure inscribed in a semicircle* as a triangle immediately yields scientific knowledge of its angle-sum without any further middle term.
key_theses: Demonstrative foreknowledge divides asymmetrically: principles require *that they are true*, proper attributes require *what the name signifies*, and primary subjects require both *what they are* and *that they are*.

In mathematical sciences of quantity, composite figures like the equilateral triangle and square first function as *proper attributes* proved to exist via *quasi-operative* constructions before serving as secondary *subjects*.
Whereas the subject is defined absolutely, a proper attribute is defined with essential dependence upon its subject, which supplies the middle term of demonstration.

When a singular or subordinate instance—such as a figure inscribed in a semicircle—is immediately recognized under its universal species, the minor premise and the demonstrative conclusion become known simultaneously in time.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 3 — On Universal Knowledge and Recognizing the Singular Triangle Inscribed in a Semicircle
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 3, Aquinas examines how the demonstrative conclusion itself is foreknown prior to syllogistic deduction and resolves the epistemological dilemma posed in Plato's *Meno*. Before a learner receives the demonstration that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, he does not know the conclusion *unqualifiedly* (*simpliciter*), yet he knows it *in a qualified sense* (*secundum quid*): just as a natural effect pre-exists virtually (*virtute*), not actually, in its efficient causes, so the conclusion pre-exists virtually in its foreknown principles. Plato erred—much like Anaxagoras in natural philosophy—by treating virtual pre-existence as actual pre-existence, inferring from the slave boy's orderly answers to geometric questions that learning is mere recollection of innate science.

Aquinas equally refutes the opposite sophistical evasion, which claimed that someone knowing *every dyad is even* knows it only of *every dyad that he knows to be a dyad* (thereby knowing nothing whatever of an unrecognized dyad such as the third part of six). Such a restriction falsifies the very form of mathematical science: geometric and arithmetical demonstrations prove theorems concerning *every* number, *every* dyad, or *every* straight line unqualifiedly, never appending the subjective restriction *which you know*. Genuine learning (*addiscere*) is the intellectual generation of science, reducing knowledge from potential, virtual, and universal containment in first principles into proper and actual cognition.
key_theses: Prior to demonstration, a scientific conclusion is unknown *unqualifiedly* (*simpliciter*) yet foreknown *virtually* (*virtute*, *secundum quid*) within its principles, which act as efficient causes of the conclusion.
Plato's *Meno* paradox mistakes virtual pre-existence in self-evident principles for actual innate possession of geometric theorems.
Mathematical premises and conclusions hold objectively of *every* triangle, number, or straight line unqualifiedly, without the psychologistic restriction *which you know*.
Learning is a genuine cognitive generation that brings the intellect from virtual, universal potency into proper, actual scientific knowledge.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 4 — What Unqualified Scientific Knowledge Is and How Demonstration Proceeds from Primary, True, Immediate Causes
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Beginning the treatise on the demonstrative syllogism proper, Aquinas explains why Aristotle constructs two linked definitions of demonstration: a formal-teleological definition taken from its end (*to know scientifically*, *scire*), which serves as the middle term proving its material definition taken from the required character of its premises. Setting aside sophistical knowing *per accidens* (such as knowing Coriscus approaching), Aquinas expounds Aristotle's three conditions for *knowing unqualifiedly* (*scire simpliciter*): knowing the cause of the thing, knowing its actual application as the cause of that effect, and knowing with certitude that it cannot be otherwise. Demonstration is accordingly defined as a *scientific syllogism* (*syllogismus scientialis*)—one whose very possession constitutes scientific knowledge—which must therefore proceed from premises that are *true*, *primary*, *immediate* (lacking any prior middle term), *better known* than, *prior* to, and *causes* of the conclusion.

Manifesting each material condition, Aquinas illustrates the impossibility of knowing falsehoods through Euclid Book X: because *to be* and *to be true* are convertible, one cannot scientifically know that the diagonal of a square is commensurable (*symmetrum*) with its side, since they necessarily lack any common numerical measure. Finally, Aquinas harmonizes the *Posterior Analytics* thesis that demonstrative premises are prior *according to nature* rather than *in relation to us* (where sensible singulars come first) with *Physics* I: in natural philosophy, material essences are hidden from us so we frequently argue *a posteriori* from sensible effects, whereas in mathematics, owing to abstraction from sensible matter, demonstrations proceed purely from formal principles in which what is better known *in relation to us* is simultaneously better known *unqualifiedly* and *according to nature*.
key_theses: Unqualified scientific knowledge (*scire simpliciter*) requires knowing the cause, its actual causal nexus with the effect, and the impossibility of the truth being otherwise.

Because *being* and *being true* are convertible, falsehoods—such as the commensurability of the square's diagonal with its side (*Elements* X)—cannot be scientifically known, nor can science arise from false or unproved premises.
Demonstrative premises must be primary, immediate, causal, and naturally prior to and better known than the conclusion.

In mathematics, unlike natural philosophy, abstraction from sensible matter ensures that formal principles better known *in relation to us* are simultaneously better known *unqualifiedly* and *according to nature*.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 5 — On the Division of Immediate Principles into Axioms, Hypotheses, and Postulates
section_summaries.argument_summary:
To clarify what makes a principle *immediate*—namely, having no prior proposition or middle term through which its predicate is proved of its subject—Aquinas first distinguishes the demonstrative proposition from the dialectical problem and proposition. Whereas the dialectician asks for either side of a contradiction indifferently from probable opinion, the demonstrator determinately assumes the true part of a contradiction (an opposition lacking any intermediate *in itself*) as known. Aquinas then unfolds Aristotle's foundational taxonomy of immediate syllogistic principles into *axioms* (*dignitates* or *maximal propositions*) and *positions* (*positiones*).

Every immediate proposition is *known through itself* (*per se nota*) in itself because its predicate belongs to the intelligible nature (*ratio*) of its subject. When its terms—such as *being*, *one*, *whole*, and *part*—are known to everyone, the proposition is an *axiom* (*dignitas*), such as non-contradiction or *the whole is greater than its part*, received by all sciences from metaphysics. When its terms require technical definition not universally known—such as *All right angles are equal*, whose immediacy rests on defining a right angle via equal adjacent angles formed by one straight line falling upon another—or when a proposition is assumed in geometry though proved in natural philosophy—such as *drawing a straight line from any point to any point*—it is received by *position*. Subdividing *position*, Aquinas distinguishes *hypotheses* (*suppositiones*), which assert *to be* or *not to be*, from *definitions* (such as the arithmetician's definition of the unit as indivisible according to quantity), which signify *what a thing is* without asserting existence, serving virtually as principles of demonstration.
key_theses: Unlike the dialectician, who interrogates either side of a contradiction from probabilities, the demonstrator determinately assumes the true part of a contradiction.
Immediate propositions whose terms (*being*, *whole*, *part*) are universally understood are *axioms* (*dignitates*), evident both in themselves and to all learners.

Propositions immediate in themselves whose technical definitions are not universally known (such as *All right angles are equal*), or principles borrowed from another science (such as drawing a straight line between any two points), belong to *positions* and *hypotheses*.

Definitions are non-propositional *positions* that signify *what a thing is* (e.g., the unit as indivisible according to quantity) without asserting *that it is*, functioning virtually as syllogistic principles.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 6 — Against Those Who Deny Demonstration or Posit Circular Demonstration
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 6, Aquinas establishes the epistemic asymmetry that renders both infinite regress and circular demonstration impossible (which Aristotle explicitly refutes immediately thereafter on this very basis): the immediate principles of a demonstration must be not merely foreknown, but *more known* and *more firmly believed* than the demonstrated conclusion. Explaining Aristotle's qualification *either all or some*, Aquinas notes that proximate geometric premises—such as Euclid I.16, that the exterior angle of a triangle equals the two opposite interior angles—are initially just as unknown as the conclusion (Euclid I.32) until resolved back into immediate principles, whereas first principles are immediately better known upon being proposed.

Aquinas expounds Aristotle's two proofs of this epistemic superiority. First, by direct causal proportionality (*propter quod unumquodque tale, et illud magis*): because we know and believe conclusions *on account of* principles, just as fire is hotter than what it heats (or the sun possesses a worthier causal power than terrestrial heat), we must know and believe the principles more than the conclusion. Second, by reduction to impossibility: if principles were not better known than a conclusion not yet known, the knower—or even one *better disposed* than a scientific knower, namely one possessing *understanding* (*intellectus*) of principles—would believe the unknown equally with or more than the known. Moreover, scientific certitude demands unshakeable adherence (*incredibilem non esse*), requiring that nothing be more certain to the demonstrator than the falsity of the principles' opposites.
key_theses: Immediate principles must be known better and believed more firmly than any conclusion demonstrated through them, precluding circular proof.
Proximate theorems (such as the exterior-angle property of a triangle) require prior proof, whereas primary axioms are immediately better known as soon as their terms are grasped.
By the causal principle *that on account of which each thing is such is itself more so*, cognitive certitude belongs pre-eminently to first principles and derivatively to conclusions.
Unshakeable scientific certitude requires absolute conviction that the opposites of first principles are false, excluding all fear of the contrary.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 17 — That No Particular Science Demonstrates Its Own Proper Principles, Which Belong to First Philosophy
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Aquinas here establishes that genuine *propter quid* demonstration requires *proper* and *proximate* principles belonging *per se* to the subject-genus, not merely true and immediate common axioms. He illustrates this failure of generic proximity through Bryson's sophistical squaring of the circle (*tetragonismus*): Bryson argued that wherever there exist something greater and something less (circumscribed and inscribed squares around a circle), there exists something equal, and hence a square equal to the circle. Because *equal*, *greater*, and *less* transcend the genus of circle and rectilinear polygon—applying equally to numbers, times, or weights—Bryson's argument yields at best *per accidens* knowledge rather than *per se* geometric causation.

Addressing the objection from subalternate sciences—such as *harmonics* (music) proved through arithmetic, or *optics* (perspective) and mechanical arts proved through geometry—Aquinas distinguishes *knowing that* (*quia*) in the lower science from *knowing the reason why* (*propter quid*) in the superior mathematical science to whose subject-genus the middle term essentially belongs. From the dual fact that particular sciences cannot demonstrate from common axioms alone and yet their proper principles presuppose higher common truths, Aquinas deduces a monumental architectural conclusion: no particular science (neither geometry nor arithmetic) can demonstrate its own proper principles; that office belongs to *first philosophy* (metaphysics), which studies *being qua being* and the common principles of all sciences as its own proper domain.
key_theses: True and immediate common premises do not suffice for science unless joined to *proper* principles proximate to the subject-genus.

Bryson's attempted quadrature of the circle fails as a geometric demonstration because its middle term (*greater, less, and equal*) transcends the proximate genus of circular and rectilinear magnitudes.

In subalternate sciences (harmonics under arithmetic, optics and mechanics under geometry), the lower science knows the *that* (*quia*) while the pure mathematical science knows the *reason why* (*propter quid*).
No particular science can demonstrate its own first proper principles; their ultimate validation belongs to *first philosophy* (metaphysics), which treats *being* universally.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 18 — On the Three Elements Required in Every Demonstrative Science: Subject-Genus, Proper Attributes, and Common Axioms
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Synthesizing the relationship between proper and common principles, Aquinas sets forth the canonical triad governing every demonstrative science. First, distinguishing principles from derived theorems (*ea quae sunt ex principiis*), he notes that while both require nominal or quidditative understanding (*quid significent*), mathematics *supposes* the existence (*quia sunt*) of its primary subjects—the *unit* and *magnitude* (points and lines)—whereas it *demonstrates* the existence of derived constructs and attributes, such as the equilateral triangle, the right angle, and the straightness of a constructed line. Second, reconciling the use of common axioms with the prohibition against generic kind-crossing, Aquinas explains that common conceptions of the mind are employed in each science *according to analogy* (*secundum analogiam*), contracted proportionally to its subject-genus: geometry restricts *subtracting equals from equals* to *equal magnitudes*, while arithmetic restricts it to *equal numbers*.

Illustrating proper principles and proper attributes across arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy, Aquinas highlights arithmetical attributes (even, odd, square, cubic) alongside rich Euclidean geometric attributes: *rational* (*commensurable*) versus *irrational* or *surd* (*incommensurable*) lines measured against a given reference line, as well as the *deflected* and the *curved*. Every demonstrative science therefore revolves around three things: the *subject-genus* (*genus subiectum*), the *common axioms* (*communes dignitates*), and the *proper attributes* (*passiones*)—even when a science omits express mention of one because it is already manifest to reason (like number) or to sense.
key_theses: Mathematics supposes both the meaning and existence of primary subjects (unit, magnitude, points, lines) while demonstrating the existence of constructed figures and proper attributes (equilateral triangle, right angle, rational and surd lines).
Common conceptions of the mind enter into particular sciences *according to analogy*, contracted proportionally to continuous magnitudes in geometry and discrete numbers in arithmetic.
Every demonstrative science necessarily rests on three pillars: the *subject-genus*, the *common axioms* (*communes dignitates*), and the *proper attributes* (*passiones*).
A science may omit explicit formulation of manifest presuppositions (such as the existence of number or familiar common notions), yet all three elements remain naturally presupposed.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 19 — On Common Conceptions of the Mind, Hypotheses, Postulates, and Why the Geometer Does Not Demonstrate of Lines Drawn in Dust
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Lecture 19 delivers Aquinas's most penetrating analysis of axiomatic foundations and geometric idealization. First, he distinguishes *common conceptions of the mind* (*communes animi conceptiones*, *dignitates*) from *hypotheses* (*suppositiones*) and *postulates* (*petitiones*). While all principles are true *per se*, common conceptions must also necessarily *be seen* to be true *per se* by the natural light of *inward reason* (*ratio interior*): although a skeptic may deny non-contradiction in *outward spoken words* (*voce*), no intellect can inwardly conceive its opposite. Hypotheses and postulates, by contrast, are demonstrable truths assumed without middle terms within a given science and differ relatively to the learner: what seems probable to the student is assumed as a *hypothesis*, what meets neutral suspension of judgment is requested as a *postulate*, and what meets contrary opinion becomes a *question* requiring prior disputation.

Second, Aquinas proves twice that *definitions* (*termini*) are neither hypotheses nor postulates, since definitions neither assert *to be* or *not to be* nor predicate universally or particularly, requiring only intellectual comprehension. Within this proof, he resolves the famous objection that geometers argue from false hypotheses when calling an imperfectly traced mark in the dust (*in pulvere*) straight or one foot long: because geometry demonstrates exclusively of universals, the geometer demonstrates neither *concerning* nor *from* sensible lines, using them merely as sensible examples through which universal natures are understood. Finally, against Platonism, Aquinas concludes that eternal geometric demonstrations require no separated Ideas (*unum extra multa*), but only a universal nature existing *one in many and predicated univocally of many* (*unum in multis et de multis*).
key_theses: Common conceptions of the mind (*dignitates*) command necessary assent from *inward reason*, whereas *hypotheses* and *postulates* are demonstrable principles assumed without proof within a science according to the learner's disposition.
Definitions (*termini*) are neither hypotheses nor postulates because they signify quidditative meaning without asserting existence or universal/particular predication.

The geometer utters no falsehood in calling a line drawn in the dust straight or one foot long, for he demonstrates neither *of* nor *from* sensible particulars, using diagrams solely as exemplars of intelligible universals.
Apodictic geometric necessity requires no Platonic separated Forms (*unum extra multa*), but only univocal universals existing *one in many*.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 42 — How One Science Is More Certain and Prior to Another: The Unit Without Position and the Point Having Position
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Following immediately upon his ranking of scientific certitude and priority by ontological simplicity—where arithmetic excels geometry because the *unit is substance without position* (*unitas sine positione*) whereas the *point adds determinate position* (*punctus habens positionem*, Lect. 41)—Aquinas in Lecture 42 establishes the lower boundary of scientific objects by excluding fortuitous events (*a fortuna*) and sensory particulars (*per sensum*). Chance events occur in a minority of cases (*ut in paucioribus*) and *per accidens*, whereas demonstration requires either *a priori* absolute necessity—characteristic of the mathematical *disciplines* (*disciplinae*), which are always true—or *a posteriori* conditional necessity from end and form (*ut frequenter*) in natural generation.

Turning to sense perception, Aquinas proves that because sensation apprehends sensible qualities inhering in a singular substance restricted to *here and now* (*hic et nunc*), it can never grasp the universal, which is *always and everywhere*—not positively as an eternal entity, but *by way of negation or abstraction* from determinate time and place. Even if we could visually perceive that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, or stood upon the moon observing the earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse, we would perceive only a singular fact and still require demonstration to know the universal *per se* cause. Sense is nevertheless ordered to science—as illustrated by the hidden pores of transparent glass—insofar as repeated visual observations yield *experience* (*experimentum*), from which the intellect grasps the universal concerning *all* instances together.
key_theses: Completing the hierarchy of exactitude anchored in the *unit without position* and the *point having position*, mathematical *disciplines* possess *a priori* necessity, whereas natural sciences possess conditional *a posteriori* necessity and fortuitous events admit of no science.
A universal is *always and everywhere* not by positive omnipresence, but *by way of abstraction* from every determinate *here and now*, placing it beyond the reach of sense.

Even direct sensory perception that a triangle's angles equal two right angles, or standing on the moon to watch the earth's shadow cause an eclipse, would not yield *scientia* without universal causal demonstration.
Sense serves science not by constituting scientific knowledge, but by supplying singular observations from which *experience* and intellectual universality arise.

section_summaries.heading: Book II, Lecture 20 — On the Origin of the Habit of First Principles (Intellectus) from Sense, Memory, and Experience
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In the crowning final lecture of the *Posterior Analytics*, Aquinas resolves how the first indemonstrable principles become known and by what intellectual habit they are held. Confronting the dilemma between innate Platonism (which absurdly posits hidden possession of a knowledge more certain than demonstration) and radical empiricism or skepticism (which cannot generate supreme certitude from total ignorance without pre-existing demonstrative knowledge), Aquinas traces a pre-existing cognitive power—innate *sense*—that is prior in the order of generation without surpassing principles in certitude. Across three grades of animal cognition, transient sensation leaves retained phantasms in *memory*, and in humans multiple memories compared by particular collative reason generate *experience* (*experimentum*). Ascending beyond particular experience, the intellect grasps the *universal resting in the soul*—one apart from the many in intellectual consideration, yet existing specifically in singulars—which serves as the principle of *art* (in things subject to generation) and of *science* (in necessary things such as *numbers and geometrical figures*), illustrated by Aristotle's famous simile of a routed army rallying soldier by soldier until a battle-line stands fast.

Crucially, Aquinas guards against sensualist reductionism: sense and memory never suffice of themselves to cause universal science unless the soul possesses both the *possible intellect* to receive universal intelligibles and the *agent intellect* to abstract universals from phantasms—enabled because sense apprehends Callias not merely as Callias, but implicitly as *this man*. Finally, comparing intellectual habits, Aquinas proves that because demonstration cannot regress infinitely, discursive *scientia* cannot know its own starting points; rather, *understanding* (*intellectus*)—the infallible *habit of principles*—apprehends first principles immediately and stands to them just as *science* as a whole stands to the entire body of demonstrated conclusions.
key_theses: First principles are neither innate habits hidden in the soul nor conclusions deduced from higher science, but arise genetic-epistemically from pre-existing sense.

From sensation arises memory, from repeated memories compared by particular reason arises *experience* (*experimentum*), and from experience the intellect grasps the *universal resting in the soul* governing numbers and figures.

Sensory induction (*inductio*) yields universal principles only through the abstractive illumination of the *agent intellect* and reception in the *possible intellect*, grounded in sense's implicit grasp of the common nature in the singular.
The habit by which first indemonstrable principles are known is *understanding* (*intellectus*), the infallible principle of *scientia*.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 1 — On the Necessity of Logic and the Most Certain Mode of Demonstration in the Mathematical Sciences
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on the opening lines of Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics* I.1 (71a1–11)—in the Greco-Latin translation of James of Venice revised by William of Moerbeke—Aquinas precedes the text with an architectural prooemium synthesizing *Metaphysics* I.1 (980b28, humanity living by art and reasonings), *De Anima* III.6 (430a26, the twofold operation of the intellect), and the Neoplatonic-Arabic canon of the extended *Organon* (including *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*, transmitted via Alfarabi, Avicenna, and Albert the Great). Where Greek commentators such as John Philoponus and Themistius contrasted didactic demonstration with Platonic *anamnesis*, Aquinas deepens the critique by linking epistemology to hylomorphic causality: Plato's denial that syllogisms *cause* science mirrors his denial that natural forms in matter *cause* generation. In expounding 71a3 (*mathematicae enim scientiarum*), Aquinas follows Robert Grosseteste's commentary in highlighting why Aristotle places *mathematicae* first in his inductive proof: mathematical demonstrations exhibit causal necessity without material contingency.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's designation of mathematics as possessing the *certissimus modus demonstrationis* directly reflects the deductive architecture of Euclid's *Elements*. Throughout the *Elements*, every theorem and construction advances *ordine geometrico* from explicitly stated first principles—Definitions, five Postulates, and Common Notions—through rigorous chains of syllogistic resolution (*analytica*). Whereas rhetorical enthymemes and dialectical probabilities falter amid singular contingencies, Euclidean proofs such as *Elements* I.32 (the interior angles of a triangle equal two right angles) or *Elements* I.47 (the Pythagorean theorem) exemplify the *judicative* part of logic in which formal syllogistic validity (*Prior Analytics*) unites with *per se* necessary matter (*Posterior Analytics*), leaving zero room for fear of the opposite (*formido alterius*).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter I of *De Noetica Geometriae* (citing *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 1, no. 10), Peter Hoenen S.J. underscores that both Aristotle and Aquinas continuously hold geometry before their eyes as the *archetype of demonstrative science* (*typus scientiae*). Against nineteenth- and twentieth-century Hilbertian formalism and logical positivism—which sever formal syntax (*Prior Analytics*) from intelligible content (*Posterior Analytics*) and reduce geometry to an uninterpreted game of *termini transcendentes*—Hoenen invokes Aquinas's prooemium (and Chapter V's analysis of *logica utens*) to show that *judicative resolution* requires both formal consequence and *materia necessaria*: real quidditative nexus apprehended in continuous quantity.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's distinction in this prooemium between the *inventive* (*investigative*) and *judicative* (*resolutory*) moments of reason maps with striking precision onto the dual architecture of the GEOMETOR ecosystem. In *geometor.explorer* and *geometor.divine*, automated scanning across constructive configurations performs an *inventive* search that uncovers candidate golden sections, harmonic ranges, and proportional symmetries; yet discovery alone does not yield scientific certitude until *geometor.model* and *geometor.elements* execute *resolutory* verification in exact symbolic algebra via SymPy, resolving polynomial and radical identities back to primary algebraic and geometric definitions without floating-point approximation.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 2 — On the Twofold Foreknowledge (That It Is and What It Is) of Subject and Attribute: Unit and Triangle
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing *Posterior Analytics* I.1 (71a11–29), Aquinas resolves a classic exegetical puzzle already debated by Themistius, Philoponus, and Grosseteste: why Aristotle cites *unit* (*monas*) as requiring foreknowledge of both *what it is* and *that it is*, while citing *triangle* (*trigonon*) as requiring foreknowledge only of *what the name signifies* (*quid est quod dicitur*). Drawing upon *Metaphysics* IV.4 and VII.4–17, Aquinas explains that in accidental sciences of quantity—unlike metaphysics or physics, whose substantial subjects can never be attributes—an accidental form can stand as a *proper attribute* (*passio*) of a prior quantitative subject while serving in turn as the *subject* of subsequent attributes, terminating without infinite regress in primary quantitative subjects (*unitas*, *linea*, *superficies*). He likewise clarifies Aristotle's distinction at 71a17–24 between temporal foreknowledge of the major premise and simultaneous recognition (*hama epagomenos*) of a singular under its species.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: This lecture contains Aquinas's explicit philosophical explanation of the architecture of Book I of Euclid's *Elements*. Quoting *Elements* I.1 verbatim (*super rectam lineam datam triangulum aequilaterum constituere*) and referencing *Elements* I.46 (construction of the square), Aquinas characterizes Euclidean constructive problems as *quasi-operative demonstrations* (*demonstrationes quasi operativae*). Euclid presupposes the existence and nominal definitions of points, straight lines, surfaces, and circles (Postulates 1–3), uses them in I.1 to *demonstrate the mathematical existence* of the equilateral triangle from its nominal definition (Def. 20), and thereafter treats the constructed triangle as a subject to prove *proper attributes* such as the equality of its angles (*Elements* I.5 Cor.) and the two-right-angle sum (*Elements* I.32), instantiated immediately in a triangle inscribed in a semicircle (*Elements* III.31).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Lecture 2, no. 5 is one of Hoenen's pivotal proof-texts across *De Noetica Geometriae* (cited extensively in Chapter IV on Euclid I.1 and Chapter VII on geometric existence). Engaging Bertrand Russell's critique that Euclid illicitly assumes without continuity axioms that the two circles in *Elements* I.1 intersect at point *C*, Hoenen agrees with Russell that I.1 is an *existence proof*—just as Aquinas's doctrine of *demonstratio quasi operativa* establishes—while refuting Russell's blind formalism: mathematical existence (*esse mathematicum*, non-repugnance in continuous extension) cannot be conjured from empty symbolic postulates, because the intersection of the two circles is intellectually *intuited as necessary* in the phantasmatic continuum from the presupposed nature of *linea* and *superficies*.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's account of *quasi-operative demonstrations*, in which constructed figures transition from demonstrated *attributes* of prior lines and circles into *subjects* of downstream properties, directly mirrors the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) construction engine of *geometor.model* and *geometor.elements*. Starting from two foundational seed points (the presupposed primary subjects of position and unit distance), every subsequent straight line, circle, intersection point, equilateral triangle, or square is constructively *generated* as a derived algebraic node whose existence (real symbolic intersection roots in SymPy) is proved from ancestor elements before *geometor.divine* analyzes the resulting figure as a subject bearing emergent golden-ratio attributes.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 3 — On Universal Knowledge and Recognizing the Singular Triangle Inscribed in a Semicircle
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Posterior Analytics* I.1 (71a24–b8), Aquinas situates Aristotle's solution to the eristic paradox of Plato's *Meno* (80d–86c) within the overarching Aristotelian metaphysics of potency and act (*Physics* I.8, II.3; *Metaphysics* IX). Just as Anaxagoras posited latent actual forms in matter to avoid generation from nothing, Plato posited actual innate science in the soul because the uninstructed boy in the *Meno* (questioned on doubling the square) answered truly from self-evident principles. Against both Plato and the sophistical restrictivists criticized by Aristotle at 71a30–b5 (who restricted universal premises to *every number which you know*), Aquinas applies the causal doctrine of *Physics* II.3—where premises stand to conclusions as efficient causes to effects—showing that learning (*addiscere*) is the actualization of conclusions virtually contained in universal principles.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two celebrated Euclidean theorems frame this lecture's epistemology. First, *Elements* I.32—that every triangle has its three interior angles equal to two right angles—exemplifies a theorem virtually contained in Euclid's definitions, parallel postulate, and Common Notions prior to explicit proof, yet holding objectively of *every* rectilinear triangle unqualifiedly rather than merely of triangles previously inspected by the geometer. Second, combining Lectures 2 and 3, the recognition of a triangle *inscribed in a semicircle* recalls *Elements* III.31 (Thales' theorem that the angle in a semicircle is right): once the geometer apprehends the three bounding chords in the semicircle as forming a triangle, the universal angle-sum theorem applies instantaneously without requiring an intermediate syllogism.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen draws heavily upon this lecture's distinction between *virtual* containment in principles and *actual* scientific cognition to refute both Kantian synthetic *a priori* constructivism and tautological logicism (Frege, Wittgenstein, and logical positivism, critiqued in *De Noetica Geometriae* Chapters II and V). Against the positivist claim that all mathematical deduction is an analytic tautology saying nothing genuinely new, Aquinas's analysis of virtual pre-existence shows how synthetic geometric constructions and deductions bring the mind from potential, undifferentiated universality into genuinely new *actual* scientific knowledge, while preserving the unrestricted ontological universality (*de omni simpliciter*) of every geometric theorem.
section_notes.geometor_significance: In computational geometry and machine reasoning within GEOMETOR, the distinction between *virtual* containment and *actual* knowledge illuminates why deductive construction and symbolic evaluation are non-trivial generators of discovery. Once initial points and constructive rules are posited in *geometor.model*, every constructible intersection and every golden proportion is *virtually* determined within the algebraic field; yet those proportional truths remain epistemically latent until constructive steps in *geometor.elements* and exact symbolic simplification in *geometor.divine* reduce them from virtual algebraic potentiality into explicit, verified theorems that hold *unqualifiedly* across the entire equivalence class of the configuration.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 4 — What Unqualified Scientific Knowledge Is and How Demonstration Proceeds from Primary, True, Immediate Causes
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing *Posterior Analytics* I.2 (71b9–29), Aquinas displays classic Scholastic mastery by uniting *Physics* II.9 and *De Anima* I.1 (the final-cause definition as middle term proving the material-cause definition) with *Metaphysics* II.1 (993b30, the convertibility of *esse* and truth). Following Themistius and Grosseteste on 71b17 (*syllogismus scientialis* rendering *syllogismos epistemonikos*), Aquinas carefully distinguishes knowing *simpliciter* from sophistical knowing *per accidens* (the Coriscus fallacy of *Sophistical Refutations* 24). Most importantly, in paragraph 16, Aquinas resolves the apparent contradiction between *Posterior Analytics* I.2 (71b33–72a5, universals are remote from sense and prior by nature) and *Physics* I.1 (184a16–26, universals are better known to us), establishing a decisive epistemological boundary between natural philosophy and mathematics.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas explicitly invokes *Book X of Euclid* (*ut patet ex X Euclidis*, referencing the classic proof associated with *Elements* X.2, X.9, and the ancient appendix X.117) to illustrate Aristotle's example at 71b26 of an impossible falsehood that can never be scientifically known: that the diagonal (*diametrum*) of a square is commensurable (*symmetrum*) with its side. Defining incommensurable magnitudes with precision as quantities admitting no common measure and lacking the ratio of a number to a number (√2 : 1), Aquinas shows how geometric truth is anchored in objective quantitative being. Furthermore, Euclid's axiomatic order exemplifies how in mathematics, because sensible matter is abstracted away, formal definitions and axioms are simultaneously most intelligible *to us* and primary *in nature*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen repeatedly returns to Aquinas's teaching here (alongside *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 10 and *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 85, a. 1, ad 2 in *De Noetica Geometriae* Chapters II and VI) to explain the unique transparency of geometric causality. Unlike physical substances whose inner essences remain hidden behind sensible accidents and must be deciphered *a posteriori* from effects, mathematical forms (*numeri, dimensiones, figurae*) are abstracted from sensible qualities while retaining intelligible matter; hence the formal nexus whereby properties flow *per se* from quantitative essence—including the exact crisis of incommensurability analyzed by Hoenen in Chapter VI—is directly penetrable to human intellectual intuition.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's invocation of the incommensurability of the square's diagonal with its side (*Elements* X) strikes at the very heart of GEOMETOR's founding philosophy. Standard dynamic geometry software represents √2 and the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 as truncated binary rationals—effectively treating incommensurable magnitudes as *commensurable* ratios of integers and thereby embedding the very falsehood Aquinas declares unknowable. By grounding *geometor.model* in SymPy's exact symbolic algebra, GEOMETOR preserves the algebraic identity of quadratic and higher polynomial irrationals, ensuring that computational verification aligns with *being* and *truth*.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 5 — On the Division of Immediate Principles into Axioms, Hypotheses, and Postulates
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Posterior Analytics* I.2 (72a5–24), Aquinas synthesizes Aristotle's division of immediate principles (*archai amesoi*) into *axioms* (*axiomata*, rendered *dignitates* or *maximae propositiones* via Boethius's *De hebdomadibus* and *De topicis differentiis*) and *theses* (*theseis*, rendered *positiones*), subdivided into *hypotheses* (*suppositiones*) and *definitions* (*horismoi*). Aquinas enriches Aristotle's text with his celebrated epistemological distinction (parallel to *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 2, a. 1 and *In IV Metaph.*, lect. 6) between propositions *per se notae secundum se et quoad omnes*—rooted in *ens* as the intellect's first conception—and propositions *per se notae secundum se tantum*, whose technical terms require scientific instruction, alongside subalternated assumptions borrowed from higher sciences.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Remarkably, Aquinas maps Aristotle's logical taxonomy directly onto all three tiers of Euclid's Book I principles! First, he illustrates *dignitates* with Euclid's Common Notion 5 (*totum est maius sua parte*, the whole is greater than its part). Second, he illustrates propositions immediate in themselves through technical definition with Euclid's Postulate 4 (*omnes recti anguli sunt aequales*, all right angles are equal), grounding it explicitly in Euclid's Definition 10 (a straight line standing on a straight line making adjacent angles equal). Third, he illustrates *suppositiones* proved in another science with Euclid's Postulate 1 (*a puncto ad punctum rectam lineam ducere*), remarking that the geometer presupposes drawing a straight line between any two points while the natural philosopher proves the continuity of the intervening line (*Physics* V–VI). Finally, he cites Euclid Book VII Def. 1 on the arithmetical unit.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter I of *De Noetica Geometriae* (citing *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 5, no. 7) and Chapter IV, Hoenen highlights Aquinas's nuanced treatment of Euclid's Postulates 1 and 4 to dismantle modern axiomatic conventionalism (Poincaré and Hilbert). Modern formalists treat *axioms*, *postulates*, and *definitions* as interchangeable implicit definitions stripped of intuitive truth. Aquinas shows instead why *All right angles are equal* and *A straight line can be drawn from any point to any point* are objectively necessary truths grounded in the continuous nature of space and angle-equality, differing from Common Notions not by arbitrariness, but by requiring fuller analysis of continuous spatial definitions.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Euclid's Postulate 1 (*to draw a straight line from any point to any point*), Postulate 4 (equality of right angles via perpendicularity), and Common Notion 5 (whole greater than part) form the foundational primitives of *geometor.model* and *geometor.elements*. In *geometor.model*, definitions of points, lines, and circles carry no existential assertion on their own until constructive straightedge and compass operations instantiate them within the symbolic plane, while universal algebraic identities (*dignitates*) govern SymPy's equation-solving and simplification engine across all geometric deductions.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 6 — Against Those Who Deny Demonstration or Posit Circular Demonstration
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing *Posterior Analytics* I.2 (72a25–b4)—the immediate premise for Aristotle's refutation of both epistemological skepticism/infinite regress and circular syllogism in I.3 (72b5–73a20, Lectures 7–8)—Aquinas displays philological care by comparing James of Venice's tortuous rendering of 72a32–36 with a direct citation of the Greek text (*In Graeco planius habetur*, drawn through Moerbeke's revision and Themistius/Grosseteste). He invokes the foundational metaphysical-logical axiom *propter quod unumquodque tale, et illud magis* to prove that cognitive certitude flows causally from principles to conclusions, and anticipates Book II's doctrine of *intellectus* in explaining Aristotle's allusion to *someone better disposed than one who knows scientifically*.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas illustrates the distinction between immediate first principles and proximate demonstrated premises with utmost precision from Book I of Euclid's *Elements*: before it is demonstrated, *Elements* I.16 (*the exterior angle of a triangle is greater than—and in I.32's proof equal to the sum of—the two opposite interior angles*) is just as unknown to the beginner as *Elements* I.32 (*a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles*). Only because *Elements* I.16 and I.29 are strictly resolved back without circularity into primary Definitions, Postulates, and Common Notions—whose opposites the intellect recognizes with absolute certitude to be false—does the proof of *Elements* I.32 impart unshakeable apodictic *scientia*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter I of *De Noetica Geometriae* (citing *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 6), Hoenen emphasizes Aquinas's contrast between discursive *scientia* (Greek *episteme*) and the superior disposition of *intellectus* (*nous*) toward first principles. Against hypothetico-deductive philosophies of mathematics (such as Lakatosian fallibilism avant la lettre or Russell's claim that axioms are justified backward by their plausible consequences), Hoenen shows with Aquinas that circular or regressive justification destroys *scientia*: if first geometric principles possessed merely hypothetical or provisional credence, fear of the opposite (*formido alterius*) would infect every theorem derived from them.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's acyclic ordering of epistemic priority—where proximate lemmas like *Elements* I.16 mediate between primary axioms and downstream theorems like *Elements* I.32 without ever circling back—is structurally realized in the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) architecture of *geometor.elements* and *geometor.trees*. Every proposition in *geometor.elements* explicitly tracks its ancestral dependency graph back to root postulates and definitions, guaranteeing strict acyclicity, preventing circular reasoning, and propagating exact symbolic certitude downward from unshakeable algebraic primitives to complex geometric theorems.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 17 — That No Particular Science Demonstrates Its Own Proper Principles, Which Belong to First Philosophy
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Posterior Analytics* I.9 (75b37–76a30), Aquinas integrates Aristotle's prohibition of kind-crossing (*metabasis eis allo genos*, established in I.7) with the hierarchy of subalternated sciences (*harmonics* under arithmetic, *optics* and *mechanics* under geometry) and the architectural supremacy of *first philosophy* (*Metaphysics* IV.1–3, VI.1). Relying on the ancient commentary tradition (Themistius, Philoponus, and pseudo-Philoponus preserved in medieval scholia on *Sophistical Refutations* 11 and *Posterior Analytics* I.9), Aquinas reconstructs Bryson of Heraclea's attempted quadrature of the circle to show why a syllogism built solely from common notions (*greater, less, and equal*) lacks a proximate middle term *per se* proportioned to circular curvature.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Bryson's fallacy illuminates the profound methodological rigor of Book XII of Euclid's *Elements* (derived from Eudoxus of Cnidus) and Archimedes' *Measurement of a Circle*. Unlike Bryson, who leaped illicitly from inscribed and circumscribed squares to an equal square via a purely dialectical appeal to *greater and less*, Eudoxus and Euclid in *Elements* XII.2 (grounded in *Elements* X.1, the Eudoxian-Archimedean exhaustion lemma) remain strictly within the *proper principles of continuous magnitude*, proving area proportionality through rigorous geometric bisection of arcs and polygons. Meanwhile, Euclid's *Optics* and *Sectio Canonis* exemplify the exact subalternation of visual perspective to geometry and musical intervals to arithmetic described in paragraphs 3 and 6.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Hoenen cites *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 17, no. 4 in Chapter I of *De Noetica Geometriae* (and develops its consequences across Chapters V–VII) to establish the proper boundary between geometry and metaphysics. On the one hand, against logicism (Frege and Russell's *Principia Mathematica*), Lecture 17 proves that particular mathematical sciences cannot be deduced from purely general logical or ontological axioms alone without *proper quantitative principles* abstracted from extension—otherwise all mathematics degenerates into Brysonian *metabasis*. On the other hand, because geometry cannot demonstrate its own first principles within geometry, critical reflection on their ultimate epistemic validity belongs rightfully to noetic metaphysics.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Both halves of Lecture 17 resonate directly with GEOMETOR. First, Bryson's continuity heuristic—sandwiching a circle between smaller and larger squares without a constructive geometric middle—foreshadows numeric root-bracketing approximations, whereas *geometor.model* insists on *proper* compass-and-straightedge algebraic intersections (precisely distinguishing constructible quadratic extensions from transcendental circle-squaring). Second, Aquinas's account of subalternation—where geometry supplies the *propter quid* formal causes for *optics*, *mechanics*, and *harmonics*—animates GEOMETOR's cross-disciplinary reach into botanical *phyllotaxis* (*geometor.phyllotaxis*) and harmonic proportion.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 18 — On the Three Elements Required in Every Demonstrative Science: Subject-Genus, Proper Attributes, and Common Axioms
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing *Posterior Analytics* I.10 (76a31–b22), Aquinas systematizes Aristotle's canonical triad of every demonstrative science (*omnis scientia demonstrativa est circa tria*: *genus subiectum*, *communes dignitates*, *passiones*). Particularly significant is Aquinas's explanation of how common axioms enter particular sciences *according to analogy* (*kat' analogian*, 76a38): transcendental or trans-generic relations of equality are proportionally contracted to discrete number in arithmetic and continuous magnitude in geometry. Notice too how Aquinas expands Aristotle's brief geometric examples (*euthy*, *keklasmenon*) by introducing technical Euclidean-Arabic terminology from Campanus of Novara and Adelard of Bath—defining *rational* (*commensurable*) versus *irrational* or *surd* (*surda*) lines.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Lecture 18 reads like a structural blueprint of Euclid's *Elements*. First, the *subject-genus* comprises continuous magnitude in Books I–VI and XI–XIII (points and lines, *signa*) and discrete units/numbers in Books VII–IX. Second, the *common axioms* contracted *secundum analogiam* appear verbatim in Euclid's Common Notion 3 (*If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal*), which Euclid applies to geometric segments and areas in Book I (e.g., I.2, I.3, I.35) and to numbers in Book VII. Third, the *proper attributes* whose nominal definitions are posited and whose existence is demonstrated span Books I, VII–IX (even, odd, square, and cube numbers, VII Defs. 6–7, 18–19), and Book X Def. 3 (lines *rational* [*rhetai*] and *irrational* [*alogoi*, medieval *surdae*] relative to an assigned reference line).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter V and Chapter VII of *De Noetica Geometriae* (linking *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 15 and 18 with *Metaphysics* V and X), Hoenen examines how common axioms such as *subtracting equals from equals* function *analogically* across heterogeneous genera of quantity. Against formalist axiomatics that flatten equality into a bare syntactic equivalence relation, Hoenen emphasizes with Aquinas that equality in continuous extension (congruence and measure) and equality in discrete multitude are proportionally distinct realizations grounded in their respective *subject-genera*, and that Book X's theory of *rational* and *surd* lines arises precisely when continuous magnitude transcends discrete numerical ratios.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's highlight of Euclid Book X's *rational* versus *irrational* (*surd*) lines relative to a *given reference line* (*linea data*) directly describes the foundational coordinate and symbolic architecture of *geometor.model* and *geometor.divine*. By fixing two initial points at (0, 0) and (1, 0) as the *linea data*, *geometor.model* computes every constructible segment length as an exact SymPy expression—distinguishing rational lengths from quadratic *surds* such as √2, √3, and φ—while applying common algebraic axioms analogically to verify exact segment, area, and cross-ratio equalities across the construction.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 19 — On Common Conceptions of the Mind, Hypotheses, Postulates, and Why the Geometer Does Not Demonstrate of Lines Drawn in Dust
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Posterior Analytics* I.10 (76b23–77a9), Aquinas weaves together three landmark Aristotelian arguments: (1) the distinction between *outward spoken discourse* (*exo logos*, *ratio exterior*) and *inward discourse in the soul* (*eso logos*, *ratio interior*, cf. *Metaphysics* IV.3, 1005b23–26 against Heraclitus), proving that *communes animi conceptiones* (Boethius's rendering of Greek *koinai ennoiai*) cannot be inwardly doubted; (2) the learner-relative distinction between *suppositio* (*hypothesis*) and *petitio* (*aitema*); and (3) Aristotle's refutation of both Protagorean anti-geometric empiricism (*lineae in pulvere descriptae*, 76b39–77a3; cf. *Metaphysics* III.2, 997b35) and Platonic separated mathematicals (*ta mathematika* alongside *eide*, 77a5–9), establishing the moderate realist universal *unum in multis et de multis*.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Proclus's *Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements* explicitly cites this very chapter of Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics* to explain Euclid's tripartite division of first principles into *Definitions* (*horoi*, which assert neither universal nor particular existence), *Postulates* (*aitemata*, requested without demonstration), and *Common Notions* (*koinai ennoiai*, *communes animi conceptiones*, self-evident to inward reason). Moreover, Aquinas's defense of the geometer tracing imperfect lines *in the dust* (*in pulvere*—referring to the ancient Greek *abax* or sand-board used with compass and straightedge) vindicates Euclid's universal diagram-based method (*ekthesis*): the drawn figure *ABC* is merely a sensible sign guiding the intellect to the exact universal relation proved in the *apodeixis*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Lecture 19 (especially nos. 2, 4, and 6) stands at the heart of Hoenen's *De Noetica Geometriae* (cited in Chapter IV, line 432, and paralleled in Chapter III on Protagoras's tangent objection). Against empiricists like John Stuart Mill (who claimed geometry treats idealized approximations of physical lines) and against formalists like Hilbert and Pasch (who sought to banish visual intuition altogether because drawn diagrams can mislead), Hoenen deploys Aquinas's doctrine of the phantasm: the intellect necessarily inspects the sensible or imaginative diagram (*in pulvere* or in phantasy) as an *exemplar*, yet abstracts from its sensory imperfections so that judgment terminates objectively in exact intelligible extension (*unum in multis*).
section_notes.geometor_significance: No passage in the medieval corpus speaks more directly to GEOMETOR than Aquinas's analysis of *lines drawn in the dust* (*in pulvere*). Every pixel rendered on a computer monitor and every IEEE-754 floating-point coordinate in conventional CAD or dynamic geometry tools is a modern *line drawn in digital dust*—neither truly straight nor exact in length. In GEOMETOR, SVG renderings in *geometor.explorer* serve faithfully in Aquinas's exact role as *sensible exemplars* aiding visual intuition, while actual geometric demonstration in *geometor.model* is executed neither *concerning* nor *from* pixel approximations, but strictly upon exact universal algebraic objects in SymPy.

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 42 — How One Science Is More Certain and Prior to Another: The Unit Without Position and the Point Having Position
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: This section forms the culmination of the *Posterior Analytics* I.27–31 treatise on the hierarchy and boundaries of scientific exactitude (Lectures 41–42). In Lecture 41 (on I.27, 87a31–37), Aquinas expounded Aristotle's criterion that a science from *fewer* elements is prior to and more certain than one existing *by addition* (*ex additione*), exemplified by arithmetic's *unit without position* (*unitas est substantia sine positione*) versus geometry's *point having position* (*punctus est substantia posita*). Immediately continuing that demarcation in Lecture 42 (on I.30–31, 87b19–88a17), Aquinas contrasts the *a priori* necessity of the mathematical *disciplines* (*disciplinae*) with conditional *a posteriori* physical necessity (*Physics* II.8–9), excludes fortuitous events (*a fortuna*), defines universality *by way of abstraction* from *here and now*, and expounds Aristotle's celebrated lunar-eclipse and perforated-glass thought experiments.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Both the *unitas/punctus* criterion and Lecture 42's anti-sensualist arguments illuminate Euclid's *Elements*. Euclid's Definition I.1 (*A point is that which has no part*, supplemented in continuous geometry by spatial site) and Definition VII.1 (*A unit is that by virtue of which each existing thing is called one*, devoid of spatial site) embody the exact distinction between positioned geometric continuity and unpositioned discrete multitude. Likewise, Aquinas's insistence in paragraph 7 that *even if we could perceive by sense that a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, we would still need to seek a demonstration* explains why *Elements* I.32 cannot be established by measuring physical triangles: only the auxiliary parallel construction reveals the universal *per se* cause valid for every triangle regardless of *here and now*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In Chapter III of *De Noetica Geometriae* (*The Exactitude of Geometric Concepts*, citing *In I Anal. Post.*, lect. 42, no. 7 directly on Aristotle 87b35), Hoenen singles out this exact passage as a decisive refutation of geometric empiricism. Sensory measurements of drawn triangles can never establish exact equality to two right angles—nor can watching a single eclipse on the moon reveal universal necessity—because sense is bound to *hoc aliquid, alicubi et nunc*. Yet, as Hoenen notes alongside Aquinas's paragraph 10 on *experimentum*, sensible inspection is ordered to geometry by presenting concrete spatial configurations in which the abstracting intellect grasps universal, time- and place-independent geometric necessity.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's thought experiment in paragraph 7—that even direct visual perception of a triangle's angle-sum or of an eclipse on the moon would not constitute *scientia* without universal causal demonstration—captures the methodological division of labor between visual inspection and symbolic proof in GEOMETOR. Visually observing in *geometor.explorer* or numerically sampling in floating-point arithmetic that three lines appear concurrent or two segments appear to stand in the golden ratio φ is epistemically akin to standing on the moon watching a singular shadow: true *scientia* is achieved only when *geometor.model* and *geometor.divine* prove the identity universally and *a priori* in exact symbolic algebra, independent of any singular coordinate placement.

section_notes.heading: Book II, Lecture 20 — On the Origin of the Habit of First Principles (Intellectus) from Sense, Memory, and Experience
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expositing the famous closing chapter of the *Posterior Analytics* (II.19, 99b15–100b17, numbered Lecture 20 in the Leonine division), Aquinas harmonizes Aristotle's genetic account of *epagoge* (induction)—rising from *aisthesis* (sense) through *mneme* (memory) and *empeiria* (*experimentum*, parallel to *Metaphysics* I.1, 980a27–981a12) to the *universal resting in the soul* illustrated by the rallying of a routed army (*fuga exercitus*)—with the noetic psychology of *De Anima* III.4–5 and the intellectual virtues of *Nicomachean Ethics* VI.3–7. Against Averroistic separated-intellect readings and ancient sensualism alike, Aquinas inserts two decisive clarifications in paragraphs 12 and 14: sense implicitly perceives the universal-in-the-particular (*Callias as this man*) via the cogitative power (*ratio particularis*), and the *agent intellect* (*intellectus agens*) actively abstracts universal natures and illuminates *understanding* (*intellectus*, Greek *nous*) as the infallible habit of first principles.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Significantly, in paragraph 11 Aquinas explicitly names *numbers and geometrical figures* (*circa numeros vel figuras*) as the primary exemplars of necessary, unchanging objects whose first principles arise through this inductive-abstractive ascent! Unlike medical or agricultural rules of *art*, which generalize across mutable processes of generation, Euclidean Common Notions (*things equal to the same thing are equal to one another*; *the whole is greater than its part*) and primary definitions of straight line, circle, figure, and unit require sensory and imaginative experience of bounded extensions only so that the agent intellect may immediately behold the necessary, invariant relations of continuous quantity through the habit of *intellectus*.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Book II, Lecture 20 is the supreme epistemological cornerstone of Hoenen's entire philosophical project—both in his landmark 1933 *Gregorianum* study *De origine primorum principiorum scientiae* and throughout *De Noetica Geometriae* (explicitly cited in Chapter II, line 321, and paired with *De Veritate* q. 10, a. 6, sc. 2 in Chapters II, IV, and VII). Against Kant (who held that *experience* can never yield strict necessity and universality, forcing geometry into subjective *a priori* forms) and against Hilbertian axiomatics (which abandons intuitive truth altogether), Hoenen proves with Aquinas that the *agent intellect* abstracts from imaginative *experimentum* not merely incomplex concepts (*termini*), but necessary *judgments*—intuiting in the phantasm the intrinsic formal nexus of Euclidean axioms and postulates.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's genetic arc from singular sensations and collative *experience* (*experimentum*) to the *universal resting in the soul* and the habit of *understanding* (*intellectus*) illuminates both human geometric discovery in *geometor.explorer* and machine program synthesis in *geometor.seer*. Just as the human mind compares multiple concrete configurations (like soldiers rallying one by one in a routed army) until the intellect grasps the invariant structural law governing all instances, *geometor.seer* inspects finite visual training grids not to memorize pixel contingencies, but to abstract and synthesize a verifiable universal transformation rule—while in *geometor.divine* and *geometor.model*, empirical pattern recognition across constructive steps culminates in exact, invariant symbolic understanding.
